summary: Differentiate refill windows: separate telemetry healthchecks from bulk embed pipeline to prevent opaque 429s
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports repeated 429s that correlate with a mix of short telemetry healthchecks and large concurrent embedding uploads. The customer is running an orchestrated bulk embed pipeline (1000s of small files) plus aggressive per-host healthchecks (HTTP/2 keepalives + /health pings) from their fleet. They want guidance and a configuration that prevents telemetry traffic from consuming burst credits intended for their embed pipeline.

Impact:
- Intermittent 429s during nightly embed backfills and occasional daytime spikes that impact batch SLAs.
- Customer perceives unpredictable quota depletion; dashboards show burst pool exhaustion within minutes even when embed workers appear to be within nominal request rates.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool on prod-us-west (customer-subnet, reserved GPUs).
- Orchestrator: DataWeave batch uploader (k8s cronjob) with 48 concurrent pods.
- Telemetry: fleet health pings (every 10s per host), k8s readiness probes and an external monitoring service hitting signed URLs.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start scheduled backfill with 48 workers uploading parallel embedding jobs (each job does 20 parallel requests).
2) Keep telemetry pings enabled (10s interval) across 120 hosts.
3) Observe 429s in embed workers within ~3–7 minutes; rate-limit headers report burst window exhausted.

Observed logs and headers (redacted):
- x-ratelimit-limit: 5000
- x-ratelimit-remaining: 0
- x-ratelimit-reset: 2026-03-12T03:12:04Z
- Edge logs: token-decrement events show many small increments attributed to /health endpoints and external monitoring endpoints.
- Serving runtime traces: queue depth spikes at ingress layer then falls back to 429s at rate-limiter.

Requested outcome:
- Best-practice configuration for separating telemetry/healthcheck traffic from business-critical bulk embeds on a dedicated pool.
- Mitigation steps the customer can apply now to reduce noisy-healthcheck impact without turning off monitoring completely.

investigation_notes:
Summary of findings:
- Token accounting: healthcheck requests are small but high-frequency; they consumed ~18% of burst tokens within steady-state due to many hosts and short refill windows.
- Burst window mismatch: embed jobs expect burst credits to absorb short peaks; telemetry noise reduces effective burst capacity.
- Signed-URL preflight behavior: preflight requests from monitoring are seen as separate anonymous-origin hits (no API key), which currently map to the tenant’s primary route and token pool.
- Config gaps: dedicated control-plane supports per-path route weighting and separate burst pools but customer had a single default route for both embed and health endpoints.
Proofs and artifacts:
- Edge trace: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/edges/edge-token-decrements?orgId=1&var-tenant=DataWeave (customer-access-redacted)
resolution:
Temporary mitigations (applied via support-controlled config):
- Created a low-priority route specifically matching telemetry paths (/health, /monitoring/*, signed-url callbacks). Assigned a small sustained window and a separate burst pool (10% of original burst size).
- For embed route, increased burst pool size by 20% and lengthened refill window to smooth scheduling spikes for bulk uploads.
- Added guidance to customer: reduce host-level healthcheck frequency to 30s for non-critical hosts, aggregate readiness checks through a single proxy where possible, and configure client-side exponential backoff when 429s returned.
Longer-term recommendations / action items:
1) Implement a control-plane feature to auto-detect and suggest route separation when the ratio of small/health requests to total tokens > 10% for a sustained period. (Tracked in INT-3421).
2) Add a telemetry policy that can mark signed-url preflight traffic as monitoring-origin to route into isolated pools. (Follow-up PR: github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/512).
3) Produce customer-facing runbook for Dedicated customers on split-pool configuration and best practices (confluence page linked).
4) SRE follow-up: schedule canary rollout of new per-path pool config to one dedicated customer with similar footprint and monitor token-decrement metrics for 48h.

Notes on rollout and safety:
- All control-plane changes were implemented without GPU restart; rollback hook added to revert route mappings instantly.
- We will monitor X-RateLimit headers and token-decrement graphs and advise customer to run backfill during canary window.
resolution_status: Partial - controls applied; waiting on customer canary results
